title: When Congress Overrides the Court
hook: A high court's ruling isn't always the last word. When judges interpret a statute, the legislature can often just rewrite the law — unless the decision rests on the constitution itself.
key_points: Courts don't only strike laws down — much of their work is interpreting what a statute means, and that reading governs until it changes.
If the legislature dislikes how a court read one of its statutes, it can pass a new law to clarify or reverse the interpretation.
This 'override' is ordinary lawmaking, not a crisis — it's the branches in dialogue over what the law should say.
But a ruling decided on constitutional grounds can't be undone by ordinary legislation.
Overturning a constitutional decision takes a constitutional amendment — or the court reversing itself later.
So the key question is the basis of the ruling: statutory interpretations are reversible by lawmakers; constitutional ones are not.
content_html: It's easy to picture a supreme court as having the final say. But as SCOTUSblog examines, that's only half the story: when a court's ruling turns on how it interprets a statute — a law the legislature itself wrote — the legislature can often answer back.
extra_html: Much of a high court's work isn't striking laws down; it's deciding what an ambiguous law means. That interpretation then governs how the statute is applied. If lawmakers conclude the court read their statute wrongly — or in a way they no longer want — they can pass a new law that clarifies or rewrites it, effectively reversing the decision. This kind of "override" is ordinary legislation, not a showdown: it's the legislative and judicial branches in dialogue over what the law should say. The crucial limit is the basis of the ruling. If a decision rests on the constitution rather than on a statute, no ordinary law can undo it; reversing a constitutional ruling takes a constitutional amendment, or the court changing its own mind in a later case. That single distinction — statutory versus constitutional grounds — decides whether elected lawmakers get the last word, or whether the court does. (U.S. examples; the statutory-versus-constitutional logic recurs across constitutional democracies.)

related.title: Statute Law vs Common Law
related.hook: Not all law is written by legislators. Some of it is built up, case by case, by judges — and these two sources of law work very differently.

related.title: How Precedent Erodes
related.hook: Courts rarely kill an old ruling outright. More often it dies slowly — narrowed, distinguished, and ignored until little is left.

related.title: Checks and Balances
related.hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

related.title: Amending a Constitution
related.hook: A constitution has to last — but not freeze. Amendment rules let it change deliberately, usually demanding more agreement than an ordinary law.

prereqs.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
prereqs.hook: An idea becomes binding law only after a journey: drafting, committee review, debate, votes, and final approval.

flashcards.prompt: When can a legislature 'override' a court ruling simply by passing a new law?

choices.text: When the ruling interpreted a statute the legislature wrote
When the ruling was decided on constitutional grounds
Only when every judge agreed with the decision

flashcards.explanation_html: A statutory interpretation can be rewritten by ordinary legislation; the legislature is the author of the statute being read.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't Congress override a constitutional ruling with an ordinary law?
flashcards.back_html: A constitutional decision interprets a higher law than any statute, so changing it requires a constitutional amendment — or the court reversing itself.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a legislative override described as the branches in 'dialogue'?

choices.text: It's routine lawmaking responding to a court's reading, not a constitutional crisis
It lets the legislature fire judges it disagrees with
It forces the court to apologize for its ruling

flashcards.explanation_html: The court reads a law, the legislature answers by clarifying or rewriting it — a normal back-and-forth over what the law should mean.
